In eleven days, Nvidia lost its CEO, Anthropic pulled off the biggest IPO in history, and the Dow dropped eleven hundred points. Then Nvidia's CEO came back, and the stock jumped more than thirty percent. Here's what happened, and why it matters if you want to work on Wall Street.

November twelfth. Nvidia's board says Jensen Huang, who co-founded the company in 1993, has resigned as CEO, effective immediately, following a scandal, according to CBS News. CFO Colette Kress becomes interim CEO. The stock falls four point three percent that day.

Five days later, Nvidia reports earnings. Revenue: one hundred fifteen point eight billion dollars, up one hundred three percent from a year ago. A monster quarter. But the board says Huang isn't coming back, and the stock keeps sliding. By November eighteenth it closes at about one fifty one, roughly thirty seven percent below its October record.

Then comes Anthropic, the company behind Claude. It planned to sell shares at seventy to seventy eight dollars. Demand was so strong it priced at eighty three, and raised eighty one point three billion dollars. That's the largest IPO ever, passing SpaceX's seventy five billion in June. On day one it jumped as high as thirty four percent, and closed up seventeen.

But the same day, the market cracked. The Dow fell eleven hundred and one points and closed below fifty thousand for the first time since June. LPL Financial says ninety two percent of S and P stocks closed lower. Part of it: investors selling other AI stocks to buy Anthropic. Jim Cramer posted it plainly: people raising cash for Anthropic shares.

So is the AI boom over? Wall Street is split. Capital Economics says the tech selloff has further to run. UBS cut global stocks to neutral. But Goldman Sachs still sees the S and P 500 hitting eighty seven hundred by the end of 2027. Same data, opposite calls.

Then, the twist. On November twenty third, Nvidia's board voted unanimously to bring Jensen Huang back as CEO, saying U.S. government input gave it confidence his return poses no national security risk. Nvidia stock rose more than thirty percent. Anthropic went the other way, trading around eighty five dollars, barely above its IPO price.

The lesson for finance recruiting? A company's value isn't just its numbers. Nvidia posted record revenue and still lost over a third of its value, partly because of one person. That's key person risk. And a record IPO doesn't guarantee a hot stock. If an interviewer asks about a recent deal, know this one. Practice questions like it free at M and A Prep dot com.
